# Global Education Systems Overview
## South Asia and Middle East
Bangladesh and Pakistan feature multi-tiered education systems with governance divided among ministries and regional boards. Both face challenges such as low public funding (~2% GDP), rural-urban disparities, limited infrastructure, and gender gaps, though increasing literacy and female enrollment mark progress. Bangladesh’s curriculum is primarily in Bengali and English, with supplementary Islamic madrasahs and NGO-led non-formal programs, while Pakistan expands distance learning albeit hampered by rural connectivity. Saudi Arabia’s centrally managed system, historically religious, is undergoing substantial reforms emphasizing critical thinking, tolerance, vocational training, and STEM, funded above 5% GDP. Female education has notably advanced, with women constituting 60% of university enrollments.

# Global Education Systems Overview
## East Asia and Europe
Japan mandates education from ages 6 to 15 with high secondary attendance, balancing academics and moral education, supported by after-school cram schools; critiques focus on academic pressure and limited global focus. Russia requires 9–11 years compulsory education, offers vocational and specialized special education, and standardizes university admission via the Unified State Examination, achieving adult tertiary attainment twice the OECD average. The system aligns increasingly with Bologna Process standards but grapples with disparities outside urban centers. Russia’s higher education features unique two-tier postgraduate degrees and strict language proficiency requirements for foreign students, alongside state-driven patriotic curricula and multilingual support for minority languages.
The Netherlands offers mandatory schooling from age 5 to 16 or up to 18 for diploma completion, publicly funded contingent on quality. Primary education culminates in Cito testing to track students into VMBO (vocational), HAVO (applied sciences), or VWO (research universities), with flexible mobility among tracks. Postsecondary options include vocational training (MBO), higher professional courses (HBO), and research universities (WO). Persistent challenges include early tracking, socioeconomic disparities, and declining literacy and math performance.
South Korea’s structured 6-4-3-4 system emphasizes strong foundational education, competitive university admissions via the CSAT, and diverse high school tracks including vocational (Meister Schools). Despite nearly full employment, vocational education carries social stigma. Intense academic pressure, extensive private tutoring (hagwons), and student well-being issues are prominent; government measures regulate tutoring and promote wellness. English education is heavily prioritized, supporting international mobility. Challenges persist in social inequality, student rights, and labor market alignment.
The Czech Republic classifies higher professional schools granting “DiS.” titles and distinguishes universities as public (tuition-free for Czech-speaking first-time students), private, police, and military institutions. It employs the Bachelor-Master-Doctoral degree system with an academic year split into two semesters.
Poland’s education system features eight years of primary and 4–5 years secondary education divided into general, technical, and vocational tracks ending in the Matura exam. It mandates foreign languages and aligns higher education with Bologna Process standards. Curricular reforms promote educational quality and national identity.

# Global Education Systems Overview
## North America and Oceania
Canada’s provincially administered system mandates schooling from ages 5–7 to 16–18, governed by elected district boards. It supports diverse curricula, including International Baccalaureate, emphasizes Indigenous and anti-racism education, and invests significantly in post-secondary education (~5.2% GDP). Rigorous provincial assessments ensure standards.
New Zealand provides education from early childhood through tertiary levels, with compulsory schooling from ages 5 to 16. Māori language immersion and national frameworks like NCEA coexist with alternatives like Cambridge and IB. Despite strong overall literacy, younger students face math challenges and achievement gaps among Māori and Pacific Islanders. Bullying is a concern addressed by government policies. Funding blends government, donations, and fees, with targeted support for special needs and tertiary student loans.

# Global Education Systems Overview
## Central and Latin America
Mexico’s system spans preschool to tertiary education, mandates inclusion for special needs students, and has expanded enrollment and literacy rates. However, secondary and tertiary completion lag OECD averages. Transitioning from elite, church-controlled to secular national education, it hosts renowned universities such as UNAM and Monterrey Tech but faces rural access and teacher specialization challenges.
This synthesis underscores a diverse global educational landscape marked by governance variety, curricular priorities ranging from moral education to STEM and vocational training, funding disparities, and ongoing reforms focused on equity, inclusion, and quality enhancement. Common challenges include urban-rural divides, social inequality, academic pressure, and adaptation to labor market needs.
